claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is prepared by powder metallurgy.
Ta enrichment can be implemented by reducing one or more of Hf, Nb, Ti, or Zr correspondingly.
High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering is a suitable route for synthesizing the composition series.
The effects of Ta enrichment can be evaluated by room-temperature compression testing under matched processing conditions.
The proposed compositional variations can be kept within a single-phase stability region without elemental segregation or secondary-phase formation.
Increasing the Ta percentage in HfNbTaTiZr increases lattice distortion.
Increasing Ta content changes microstructural features such as grain size.
Increasing Ta content may change phase stability.
Greater lattice distortion caused by Ta enrichment enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Ta enrichment promotes grain-boundary stabilization and thereby increases grain-boundary strengthening.
The strengthening caused by Ta enrichment improves compressive strength relative to the equiatomic alloy.
There is a potentially optimal Ta concentration above which the strength benefit plateaus or reverses.
Excessive Ta enrichment may cause embrittlement or phase segregation that counteracts strengthening.
The predicted strengthening applies only while Ta enrichment does not produce phase separation or brittle intermetallic phases.
Microstructural analysis and fractography can complement compression testing when evaluating the composition series.
Failure to observe a statistically significant compressive-strength increase relative to the equiatomic control would falsify the hypothesis.
